## Worldview
Baghdad, the City of Peace, is not yet seventy years old and is the largest city west of China, with several hundred thousand people (estimates vary widely). It is still repairing the damage of the siege of 812–813, when al-Ma'mun's armies took it from his brother al-Amin. Al-Ma'mun has ruled from here since 819 and spends these years on campaign against Byzantium. God is one and the Quran is His word; whether that word is created or eternal is the question the caliph has made a matter of state. He favours the rational theologians of the Mu'tazila against the traditionists, and in 833 he will make every judge swear to it. Learning is prized, and patrons pay for it. Greek books in philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy are being turned into Arabic, mostly through Syriac and mostly by Christian scholars, beside Persian and Indian works. Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy are authorities to be understood and reconciled, not tested; nobody yet expects an experiment to overrule them. Astrology is a learned profession. Medicine is Galenic and in the hands of Nestorian Christian physicians. Paper is made in the city and is replacing papyrus in the offices, but every book is copied by hand. Indian numerals with a sign for zero are known to a few astronomers and are not yet used by clerks. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians live under protection and pay the poll tax. Slavery is everywhere, from household servants and singing girls to the Turkish soldiers that the caliph's brother is buying.

## People
- **Abd Allah al-Ma'mun**: Abbasid caliph since 813, in Baghdad since 819; patron of the translations and the observatories. Knows: Mu'tazilite theology and disputation, astronomy and astrology at a patron's level, the army and the Byzantine frontier. — Born 786, son of Harun al-Rashid and a Persian concubine. Away on campaign each summer from 830 (Cilicia, Cappadocia) and in Damascus and Egypt in 831–832. Dies of a fever on campaign near Tarsus on 7 August 833, months after ordering the Mihna.
- **Abu Ishaq Muhammad al-Mu'tasim**: the caliph's half-brother, commander, his successor in 833. Knows: soldiering; builds a private army of Turkish slave-soldiers (ghilman) bought in Samarkand and Baghdad. — Barely literate by the chroniclers' account, practical, respected by the troops. Moves the court to Samarra in 836. His son Ahmad will be al-Kindi's pupil.
- **al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun**: the caliph's son and frontier commander. Knows: the Jazira and the Byzantine frontier forts. — Takes Tyana in 831; in May 833 starts building a fortress base there. Passed over for the succession; dies in prison in 838 after a plot against al-Mu'tasim.
- **Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi**: mathematician, astronomer and geographer in the caliph's service. Knows: al-Jabr wa'l-muqabala (completion and balancing), solving quadratics in words with geometric proof; reckoning with the nine Indian digits and zero; an astronomical table on the Sindhind model; a geography revising Ptolemy's coordinates. — Born c. 780, origin in Khwarazm (the nisba may only be ancestral). Associated with the House of Wisdom; reported present at the Shammasiyya solstice observations of 828. Dies c. 850. His algebra was dedicated to al-Ma'mun and is new; how far clerks use it is unknown. His Picture of the Earth (geography) is usually dated to these years, finished by about 833.
- **Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi**: young Arab aristocrat and scholar at court, later 'the philosopher of the Arabs'. Knows: what the translators bring him, Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Indian numerals; will write on optics, music, medicine dosage, cryptanalysis, perfumes and swords. — Born c. 800 in Kufa or Basra to a family of the Kinda tribe; his father governed Kufa. Under al-Ma'mun he is beginning; his main work falls under al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq. Directs translators rather than translating himself.
- **Muhammad, Ahmad and al-Hasan ibn Musa ibn Shakir (the Banu Musa)**: three brothers, sons of a former highwayman turned astronomer, raised at court as wards of al-Ma'mun. Knows: geometry, astronomy, mechanics; later famous for the Book of Ingenious Devices (c. 850) and for hiring translators with their own money. — Young in 830 (Muhammad born before 803), under the guardianship of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi. Ahmad is the mechanician, al-Hasan the geometer, Muhammad the astronomer and later the politician. Later sources credit them with a share in the degree measurement; doubtful at their age.
- **Yuhanna ibn Masawayh**: Nestorian Christian physician to the caliph, teacher of medicine. Knows: Galenic medicine, drugs and aromatics, eye disease (writes the first Arabic book on ophthalmology, Daghal al-'ayn); later dissects apes for anatomy. — Born c. 777, son of a pharmacist from Gondeshapur. Sharp-tongued; famously sends away a student who asked too many questions, Hunayn. Dies in Samarra in 857.
- **Hunayn ibn Ishaq**: young Christian (Ibadi) scholar from al-Hira, translator in the making. Knows: Syriac, Arabic, increasingly Greek; Galen. — Born 808 or 809, son of a pharmacist. After his dismissal by Ibn Masawayh he goes abroad (Byzantine lands or Alexandria) to learn Greek; when exactly he returns is uncertain, probably by the late 820s or early 830s. Works first for physicians and for the Banu Musa; his great Galen translations come in the 840s to 870s.
- **Bukhtishu ibn Jibril**: court physician, head of the richest Christian medical family. Knows: Gondeshapur medicine, court politics. — His father Jibril, physician to Harun and al-Ma'mun, died c. 827. Bukhtishu serves the caliphs on and off until his death in 870.
- **Salmawayh ibn Bunan**: Nestorian Christian physician to al-Ma'mun, then to al-Mu'tasim. Knows: Galenic clinical medicine. — Presumably in the caliph's train on campaign. Al-Mu'tasim calls him father and prays over his grave when he dies in 840.
- **Sahl ibn Harun**: secretary, writer and head of the caliph's library (Khizanat al-Hikma). Knows: Persian court literature and adab; the library's holdings. — Persian by origin; with a colleague, Salm, he runs the palace library that later sources call the Bayt al-Hikma. Famous for an essay praising thrift. Usually said to die in AH 215 (830), so meet him early.
- **al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar**: translator of Greek mathematics. Knows: Euclid's Elements (he made one version for Harun and an improved one for al-Ma'mun) and the Almagest, translated through Syriac about 827–829. — Reachable in Baghdad; little else is known of his life.
- **Yahya ibn Abi Mansur**: Persian astronomer of a Zoroastrian family (the Banu al-Munajjim), Muslim since about 818; head of the observations at Shammasiyya. Knows: Persian and Indian astronomy, the new observations behind the 'verified' tables (al-Zij al-Mumtahan). — Leads the Baghdad observations of 828–829. Dies in the caliph's train near Aleppo; the year is given as 830 or 832, so meet him early.
- **Sanad ibn Ali**: astronomer and instrument maker; built the observatory near the Shammasiyya gate. Knows: instruments (armillary, mural quadrant), observing, the arithmetic of tables. — A Jewish convert to Islam. Takes part in the observations at Baghdad and Damascus. Still alive in the 860s.
- **Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Marwarrudhi**: astronomer, leads the observations on Mount Qasiyun at Damascus. Knows: solar and lunar observation. — Observes at Damascus in 831–833 while the caliph is in Syria; later sources name him in the degree measurement.
- **Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi**: maker of astrolabes and instruments. Knows: making and using astrolabes; writes a treatise on the astrolabe. — Named with Khalid in the measurement of a degree of the meridian. A craftsman who can build what a player draws in brass.
- **Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi**: astronomer from Merv ('the calculator'). Knows: astronomical tables, the shadow functions (tangent and cotangent) in their early form, eclipse timing from star altitudes. — Observes for al-Ma'mun and lives on past 869, reportedly to a hundred.
- **al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari**: geometer and astronomer. Knows: commentary on Euclid; attempts a proof of the parallel postulate. — Takes part in the Baghdad observations of 829–830 and the Damascus ones.
- **Abu Uthman al-Jahiz**: writer from Basra, Mu'tazilite, pupil of al-Nazzam. Knows: everything that interests him, animals, people, rhetoric, trades; observes ants, pigeons, and fish in his rich, rambling style. — Born c. 776, comes to Baghdad under al-Ma'mun, who admires his writing. His Book of Animals is written much later (c. 847). Dies 868/869.
- **Ibrahim ibn Sayyar al-Nazzam**: Mu'tazilite theologian and poet. Knows: denies Abu al-Hudhayl's atoms, holds that bodies are infinitely divisible and that motion crosses them by 'leaps'; sceptical of reports he cannot check. — In Baghdad. Dies some time between 836 and 845.
- **Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf**: elder of the Basra Mu'tazila. Knows: kalam atomism, indivisible parts and accidents; disputation. — Very old by 830; dies c. 841, reportedly near a hundred years old.
- **Bishr al-Marisi**: Hanafi jurist and theologian, the old champion of the created Quran. Knows: kalam and Hanafi law; was arguing the created Quran under Harun, decades before the caliph adopted it. — Born c. 755, hated by the traditionists. Dies in Baghdad in Rajab AH 218 (August 833), the summer the Mihna begins; some modern summaries give 813 in error.
- **Ahmad ibn Hanbal**: traditionist and jurist, the leading opponent of the created Quran. Knows: tens of thousands of prophetic reports, their chains of transmission. — Born 780, teaching in Baghdad. Refuses the Mihna in 833, is sent in chains toward the caliph, who dies before he arrives; flogged under al-Mu'tasim in 834 or 835 (sources differ) and released.
- **Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad**: Mu'tazilite jurist and courtier. Knows: kalam, the case for the created Quran, the court. — Al-Ma'mun recommends him to his successor; under al-Mu'tasim he replaces Yahya ibn Aktham as chief judge (833–848) and runs the Mihna.
- **Yahya ibn Aktham**: chief judge (qadi al-qudat) and close companion of al-Ma'mun. Knows: law, the court. — Travels with the caliph. Replaced by Ibn Abi Du'ad on al-Mu'tasim's accession; chief judge again under al-Mutawakkil from 851.
- **Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi**: Tahirid chief of police (sahib al-shurta) and in effect governor of Baghdad, c. 822–850. Knows: the city, its markets, prisons and quarters. — Executes the Mihna in Baghdad by the caliph's letters of 833. Guardian of the Banu Musa.
- **Abdallah ibn Tahir**: governor of Khurasan from 828. Knows: Khurasan, irrigation law (has jurists compile a book on qanat rights). — Rules from Nishapur; beyond reach except by letter or a long road.
- **Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi**: young hadith scholar from Balkh in Baghdad. Knows: traditions; despises the philosophers. — Born 787. Ibn al-Nadim says he turned to astrology at 47 after a quarrel with al-Kindi, which would be about 832–834. Becomes the most read astrologer of the Middle Ages.
- **Ishaq al-Mawsili**: court musician and boon companion. Knows: Arabic music theory and practice, the court's gossip. — Born 767; in favour with al-Ma'mun. Dies 850.
- **Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi**: the caliph's uncle, singer, briefly rival caliph (817–819). Knows: music, the Abbasid family. — Pardoned and living in Baghdad.
- **Giwargis II and Sabrisho II**: successive Catholicoi of the Church of the East, seated in Baghdad. Knows: the Nestorian church, its schools, physicians and scribes. — Giwargis holds office from 828 to about 830–831, Sabrisho from 831 to 835. The patriarch is the official head of the caliph's Christian subjects of this church.
- **Leo the Mathematician**: Byzantine scholar in Constantinople. Knows: Euclid and Greek mathematics, astronomy. — Elsewhere. A later Byzantine story has al-Ma'mun write to the emperor Theophilos asking for him; the date is doubtful and it may belong to al-Mu'tasim's reign.

## Events and timeline
- Each summer: the army leaves for the Byzantine frontier; Tigris and Euphrates floods in spring, low water and heat (well over 40 °C) from June to September.
- 827 (AH 212): al-Ma'mun publicly declares the Quran created and Ali the best of men after the Prophet.
- c. 827–828: Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik and Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi measure a degree of the meridian in the plain of Sinjar, about 56 2/3 Arabic miles (reports give 56 to 57; the date is not fixed).
- 828 (AH 213): solstice observations at the Shammasiyya quarter of Baghdad under Yahya ibn Abi Mansur; al-Khwarizmi is reported present. Abdallah ibn Tahir becomes governor of Khurasan.
- 829: Theophilos becomes Byzantine emperor. Observations at Shammasiyya continue into 829–830.
- 829/831–832 (start disputed): the Bashmurite revolt of Christian Copts in the Nile delta, crushed when the caliph comes to Egypt with al-Afshin.
- 830 (AH 215) spring–summer: al-Ma'mun leads his first personal campaign into Byzantine territory, the first by a caliph in twenty years, takes Majida by surrender and storms and razes Qurra (July 830); Sundus also falls. Yahya ibn Abi Mansur dies in his train near Aleppo (830, or 832).
- 831: second campaign; Heraclea Cybistra and Tyana surrender. Observations on Mount Qasiyun at Damascus begin.
- 831 10 Jul: Zubayda, Harun's widow and al-Amin's mother, dies in Baghdad.
- 832: the frontier fortress of Loulon falls after a long siege (date disputed); al-Ma'mun in Egypt to end the Bashmurite revolt.
- 833 spring (AH 218): from Raqqa and the frontier the caliph writes to Ishaq ibn Ibrahim in Baghdad: judges and traditionists must declare the Quran created or lose office. The Mihna begins. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refuses and is sent in chains to the caliph.
- 833 25 May: al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun crosses into Byzantine territory and begins building a fortress at Tyana.
- 833 7 Aug (some sources 9 Aug): al-Ma'mun dies of a fever on campaign near Tarsus and is buried there. Al-Mu'tasim is proclaimed, abandons the campaign and razes Tyana.
- 834 or 835: Ahmad ibn Hanbal is questioned before al-Mu'tasim, flogged and released. The Zutt of the southern marshes are defeated and deported (834/835). Babak's Khurramite revolt in Azerbaijan, going since 816, goes on until 837.
- 836: al-Mu'tasim moves court and Turkish army to the new city of Samarra.
- 848–851: al-Mutawakkil abandons the Mihna; Yahya ibn Aktham is chief judge again from 851.

## Quest hooks
- Al-Khwarizmi's new book solves inheritance shares by al-jabr; the clerks of the land-tax office still reckon on their fingers. Race one with the nine digits and zero, on paper, before the diwan.
- A copyist in the Suq al-Warraqin spends three months on a single Galen; show what carved wooden blocks and paper could do, and find out who would want a hundred identical copies of anything.
- The astronomers measuring a degree need a better instrument, and Sanad ibn Ali will build in brass what is drawn clearly enough.
- Ibn Masawayh has never tested one remedy against another: the bimaristan has the patients for a fair trial, if someone can explain why to compare.
- The perfumers distil rose water in alembics. Push the still further, to strong spirit, and decide what to tell anyone about burning wine.
- A glassmaker in Karkh grinds a clear lump; can it be made into a lens for an old scribe's failing eyes?
- The Mihna is coming in 833. A protector who swears the Quran is created may not protect for long; a traditionist who refuses may be flogged. The player knows both outcomes.
- Al-Ma'mun dies in August 833 of a fever after eating fresh dates and drinking cold water by a river (the chroniclers' story). The player could try to change what he eats and drinks, or not.
- The salt is rising in the southern fields of the Sawad. Explain drainage before it is too late for a village.
- A Basra merchant sailing for China wants a way to find his way when the stars are clouded.
- The Banu Musa are young, rich and bored. Give them a problem worth their money, an automaton, a pump, a clock that runs at night.
- Al-Kindi is collecting Greek books on mirrors: does light go out from the eye or come in to it?
- The caliph's brother is buying Turkish slave-soldiers. Military advice given to him decides the next half-century of the caliphate.
- A Byzantine prisoner from the frontier is a mathematician. Exchange, ransom or keep him?
- Gondeshapur still trains physicians: is there a cleaner way to run a ward? Washed hands, boiled water, separate rooms for fevers.

## Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/medicine.md)
- `opium_analgesia` (Pain relief with opium and willow bark (laudanum, morphine, aspirin)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Opium (afyun) is a staple of the druggists, known from Dioscorides and Galen and compounded into theriac (tiryaq), which the caliph's physicians prepare with ceremony. Doses are by eye; overdose is known to kill. Willow is used for fever in Dioscorides. Local: Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a compounder of drugs; theriac makers of the court.
- `sanitation_sewerage` (Latrines and sewers (keeping excrement out of water, food and soil)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Islamic purity law is strict about excrement and urine, and houses have latrines over cesspits; the better quarters have covered drains to the canals. Waste still ends in the canals and the Tigris that the city drinks. Local: cesspit cleaners; jurists on purity (tahara).
- `wound_care` (Wound care (stop bleeding, clean, tie vessels, leave dirty wounds open)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Surgeons (jarrahun) suture, splint, cauterise and dress wounds with wine, vinegar, oils and honey after Galen and Paul of Aegina, known through Syriac. Cautery (kayy) is the great remedy. The armies on the Byzantine frontier take physicians, never enough. Local: jarrahun attached to the caliph's army; Bukhtishu ibn Jibril.
- `boiled_water` (Boiling drinking water and protecting wells): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Galenic and Hippocratic texts rank waters and advise boiling bad ones; the rich cool water in porous jars and ice is carried to the palaces. Most people drink Tigris and canal water brought by water carriers. Fuel is dear in a city without forests. Local: water carriers (saqqa'un) drawing from the Tigris; Airs, Waters, Places in Syriac and early Arabic versions.
- `childbirth_care` (Safe childbirth (clean hands, patience, cord care, forceps)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Midwives (qawabil) deliver on birthing stools; male physicians give advice from Galen and Soranus but rarely attend. No forceps. Childbed fever is common and blamed on retained humours. Local: midwives of the harem and the city quarters.
- `dental_care` (Tooth decay and dental care): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The miswak chewing stick (arak twig) is used several times a day as prophetic practice. Tooth worms are blamed for decay; sugar is a luxury of the rich, and their teeth show it. Extraction is the barber's job. Local: miswak sellers at the mosque gates.
- `parasitic_worms` (Parasitic worms (hookworm, roundworm, tapeworm, guinea worm)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Physicians distinguish long, round and small worms (Greek tradition) and think they breed from corrupt humours. Remedies like pomegranate root and male fern work. The guinea worm (al-irq al-madani) is known from Hijaz; transmission by water and soil is unknown.
- `anatomy_dissection` (Human anatomy from dissection): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Anatomy is Galen's, read in Syriac and early Arabic summaries. Human dissection is unthinkable to jurists. Yuhanna ibn Masawayh is later reported to dissect apes, one sent from Nubia to the court in 836. Local: Yuhanna ibn Masawayh; Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a young man hunting for Greek copies of Galen.
- `clinical_thermometer_stethoscope` (Physical diagnosis (percussion, stethoscope, thermometer, pulse count)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:high. Physicians take the pulse after Galen's many kinds and inspect urine in a flask (tafsira). Temperature is judged by hand and nobody counts beats against a clock; a pulse watch is the water clock.
- `nursing_hospital_hygiene` (Hospital hygiene and trained nursing): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:high. Baghdad has a bimaristan from Harun al-Rashid's reign, probably founded by the Barmakid vizier Yahya ibn Khalid; the story of Jibril ibn Bukhtishu founding it is doubted. Physicians are salaried and the sick are fed, but there is no idea of cleaning between patients or separating fevers. Local: the bimaristan of Baghdad; Bukhtishu ibn Jibril; Gondeshapur in Khuzistan, the physicians' home tradition.
- `first_aid_resuscitation` (First aid and resuscitation): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Bleeding is stopped by pressure, cautery and styptics; drowning victims are turned and shaken. Chest compression and mouth-to-mouth breathing are unknown.
- `food_hygiene` (Food hygiene (cooking, flies, carriers)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Ritual slaughter drains blood, pork and carrion are forbidden, and the market inspector (sahib al-suq or muhtasib) checks weights and spoiled goods. Flies, cooks' hands and carriers are no one's concern. Local: market inspector of Karkh; cookshops and harisa sellers.
- `hand_hygiene` (Hand washing with soap): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Ritual ablution (wudu') before each of five daily prayers makes hand and face washing a habit of every Muslim; hands are washed before and after meals, often with ushnan (saltwort ash). Nobody links hands to fever, and physicians and midwives do not wash between patients. Local: ablution basins at the Friday mosques; ushnan sellers.
- `contagion_theory` (Contagion by invisible living agents (germ theory)): K1 use:none make:medium acc:low. Disease comes from humoral imbalance, corrupt air (waba') and God's decree. Two sayings of the Prophet pull against each other, 'there is no contagion' and 'flee from the leper as you flee from a lion', and scholars argue over how to reconcile them. Nobody proposes living agents. Local: hadith scholars such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal; court physicians Yuhanna ibn Masawayh and Bukhtishu ibn Jibril.
- `malaria_mosquito` (Malaria carried by mosquitoes (drainage, nets)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Tertian and quartan fevers are well described by Galen and rife in the marshes of southern Iraq around Basra and Wasit, blamed on the air of stagnant water. People sleep on roofs and under nets against gnats, for comfort, not for fever. Local: the Batiha marshes between Wasit and Basra; al-Jahiz, a Basran with sharp eyes for insects.
- `quarantine` (Quarantine and isolation of the sick): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. A saying of the Prophet orders that one should not enter a land where plague (ta'un) is, nor flee from it, and Umar is said to have turned back from plague-struck Syria in 639. It is read as trust in God rather than isolation, and the great plague waves ended in Iraq around 749. Local: hadith scholars; the story of Umar and the plague of Amwas.

Blown and moulded glass of plant ash and sand is made in Iraq, Syria and at Raqqa; bottles, lamps, inkwells and vessels for perfumers and physicians. Window glass is rare. Paper has been made in Baghdad since about 794–795; tradition credits the Barmakids, and the story of Chinese prisoners at Talas is a later legend. Al-Ma'mun's surveyors measured one degree of meridian in the plain of Sinjar (c. 827), about 56 2/3 Arabic miles; the length of the mile, and so the result, is still argued. The Sun's yearly circle is tilted about 23 1/2 degrees; Shammasiyya observers measure the obliquity afresh as about 23°33', smaller than Ptolemy's 23°51'. - `eclipse_prediction` (Cause and prediction of eclipses): K3 use:correct make:medium acc:high. Court astronomers compute eclipses from the Almagest and Indian tables, and the caliph's men record observed ones to test the tables. - `tides` (Tides caused by Moon and Sun): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Basra lives by the tide in the Shatt al-Arab, twice daily, and sailors tie it to the Moon. Abu Ma'shar will write the Moon theory of tides later; for now it is practical knowledge. Local: Basra boatmen and the tidal canals.
- `wave_nature_light_sound` (Waves - sound and light): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. String ratios are known to court musicians and in Greek harmonic texts; al-Kindi will write the first Arabic music theory. Sound as moving air is Aristotelian; light as a wave is unheard of. - `ball_bearings` (Ball and roller bearings): K0 make:hard acc:medium. Axles turn in wooden or bronze sockets greased with fat or oil. Rollers under heavy stones are known to builders.

- `rolling_mill` (Rolling and slitting mill): K0 make:hard acc:low. Sheet metal is hammered; coin blanks are cast and struck by hand at the Baghdad mint. Local: Madinat al-Salam mint (dar al-darb).

## Mathematics & measurement (`math`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/math.md)
- `abacus_counting_board` (Abacus and counting board): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Clerks reckon by finger positions (hisab al-yad, 'arithmetic of the hand') and in their heads; letters of the abjad stand for numbers in astronomy. The Indian dust board is the scholars' tool. No bead frame. Local: katibs of the diwans. Elsewhere: China (counting rods); Byzantium (pebble boards).
- `fractions_rule_of_three` (Common fractions and the rule of three): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Clerks express fractions in the Arabic named fractions (a half, a third ... a tenth) and their products, astronomers in sexagesimal minutes and seconds. The rule of three is in the Sindhind and used daily for inheritance shares, which Islamic law makes an arithmetic problem. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (inheritance problems in al-Jabr); qadis and faradi (inheritance reckoners).
- `geometry_proof` (Deductive geometry and proof (Euclid, Pythagoras)): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Euclid has been translated twice by al-Hajjaj ibn Matar (for Harun and again for al-Ma'mun). Proof is admired at court and needed for astronomy; most surveyors and architects still work by rule of thumb. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar; al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari (commentary on Euclid, tries to prove the parallel postulate); the Banu Musa (young).

Archimedes' 3 1/7 is standard; al-Khwarizmi's mensuration chapter also reports Indian rules for the circle. Better digits are of no practical use yet; the Banu Musa will later write on measuring plane and spherical figures. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. Elsewhere: India (Aryabhata, 3.1416); China (Zu Chongzhi).
- `quadratic_cubic_equations` (Solving quadratic and cubic equations): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Al-Khwarizmi's six standard forms with rules and geometric proofs by completing the square are the newest mathematics in the world, dedicated to al-Ma'mun. Only positive roots count. Cubics are unsolved (Omar Khayyam will solve them geometrically c. 1070). Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.
- `solar_calendar_leap_years` (Solar calendar with leap years): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:low. The Hijri year is lunar and cannot be changed. Kharaj is collected by the Persian solar year of 365 days with no leap day, so Nawruz and the tax date drift through the seasons and farmers are taxed before harvest. Syriac Christians keep the Julian year with its leap day. Local: katibs of the diwan of the kharaj; Catholicos of the Church of the East (Julian computus).
- `square_roots_irrationals` (Square roots and irrational numbers): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:medium. Root extraction is taught in Indian reckoning and needed in al-Jabr. Euclid book 10 on irrational magnitudes is in al-Hajjaj's translation, read by very few. Roots are approximated and treated as magnitudes, not numbers. - `surveying_triangulation` (Surveying, levelling and triangulation): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Canal engineers (muhandisun) level with water levels and sighting staffs for the Sawad's irrigation grid, a craft inherited from the Sasanians. Al-Ma'mun's astronomers measure a degree of meridian in the desert by rope and star altitude, about 56 2/3 Arabic miles. - `trigonometry` (Trigonometry): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The Indian sine (jayb, from Sanskrit jya) has replaced Ptolemy's chords in the new tables. Habash al-Hasib is introducing tables of the 'shadow', our tangent and cotangent, in these years. Spherical trigonometry is still Ptolemy's and Menelaus' theorem. Pen-and-paper Indian arithmetic is a century away (al-Uqlidisi, c. 952). Paper is already cheap here, so the method can be skipped ahead. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (book on Indian reckoning); katibs of the diwan of the kharaj.

- `prime_numbers_number_theory` (Prime numbers and number theory): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Euclid's arithmetic books (7–9) with the infinity of primes are in Arabic. Nicomachus' Introduction to Arithmetic is known through Syriac; Thabit ibn Qurra, who will translate it and find the rule for amicable numbers, is a small child in Harran. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar. Elsewhere: Harran (Thabit ibn Qurra, born 826 or 836).
- `symbolic_algebra` (Symbolic algebra): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Al-Jabr is brand new, written entirely in words ('a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine dirhams'). Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa'l-muqabala, c. 820s). Elsewhere: India (Brahmagupta's colour-syllable abbreviations).

The secretaries of the diwans still reckon on their fingers and write sums out in words. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; astronomers of the Shammasiyya observations. Elsewhere: India (place value with zero since the 5th–7th c.).
- `compound_interest_exponential_growth` (Compound interest and exponential growth): K1 use:none make:easy acc:low. Interest (riba) is forbidden in law, so nobody compounds it openly. Chess (shatranj) is the fashion at court, and the doubling-grains story belongs to it, but in surviving Arabic texts only later.
- `coordinate_geometry` (Coordinate geometry and graphs of functions): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Places are fixed by longitude and latitude, in Ptolemy's Geography and in al-Khwarizmi's coordinate list for a map of the world. Graphing a relation between two quantities is unknown. - `linear_equations_matrices` (Systems of linear equations (elimination and matrices)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Brahmagupta's rules for 'fortunes and debts' sit inside the Indian astronomy behind the Sindhind, but nobody here takes them up. - `normal_distribution_errors` (Errors of measurement, the bell curve and least squares): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Al-Ma'mun's astronomers repeat solstice and equinox observations because single ones disagree, and compare instruments. Choosing between values is by judgement; there is no theory of error. - `perspective_technical_drawing` (Linear perspective and technical drawing): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. - `complex_numbers` (Complex numbers): K0 make:easy acc:low. A negative under a root means the problem 'is impossible'; al-Khwarizmi says so of the equation with no solution.

## Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/ideas.md)
- `golden_rule_universal_ethics` (Golden rule and universal ethics): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The hadith that none believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself is widely quoted; the brother is usually the fellow believer. Christians quote the Gospel version.
- `atomism` (Atomism (matter is made of tiny particles in motion)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Abu al-Hudhayl teaches that bodies are made of indivisible parts (al-juz' alladhi la yatajazza') whose properties God creates; al-Nazzam rejects atoms for infinite divisibility. It is theology, not chemistry, but it is the most atomist city in the world. Local: Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf; Ibrahim al-Nazzam.
- `measurement_quantification` (Measurement and quantification): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The court measures the heavens, the size of the earth and the Nilometer at Fustat; mints assay coin by weight and touchstone. In medicine dosage is measured, but nobody measures heat, pulse or growth. Local: Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi; mint assayers. Elsewhere: Fustat (Nilometer on Roda Island, rebuilt 861).
- `source_criticism` (Source criticism (testing documents and reports)): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Hadith scholars judge reports by their chains of transmitters (isnad) and collect information on every transmitter's honesty and memory; Yahya ibn Ma'in in Baghdad is the great critic of men. Criticism of the text itself (matn) is rarer. A player can ride this method into other fields. Local: Yahya ibn Ma'in; Ahmad ibn Hanbal; Muhammad ibn Sa'd (biographical dictionary of transmitters).
- `human_equality_dignity` (Human equality and dignity): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Islam proclaims believers equal before God, and Persian converts (the Shu'ubiyya) argue that Arabs have no claim above them. Law ranks free over slave, man over woman and Muslim over dhimmi. Local: Sahl ibn Harun (Shu'ubi sympathies); al-Jahiz (who argues the other side, and on the Zanj).
- `religious_tolerance` (Religious toleration and freedom of conscience): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians are protected dhimmis who pay jizya and stand below Muslims in law; Christians serve as physicians and secretaries at court. Manichaeans (zindiqs) were hunted down under al-Mahdi, and apostasy is death. Local: Catholicos of the Church of the East in Baghdad; Bukhtishu ibn Jibril, Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (Christian physicians).
- `formal_logic` (Formal logic (valid deduction and fallacies)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Aristotle's Categories, On Interpretation and Prior Analytics are studied by Syriac Christian scholars and partly in Arabic. Kalam debaters use dialectic (jadal) more than syllogism; jurists argue by analogy (qiyas). Local: Catholicos's circle and Syriac schools in Baghdad; Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi.
- `natural_causes` (Natural causes (naturalism about disease, weather, comets)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Aristotle's Meteorology explains rain, thunder and comets naturally, and astronomers predict eclipses. For the Mu'tazila God acts through natures; for their opponents God creates each event directly. Popular belief adds jinn, the evil eye and stars. Local: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi; Ibrahim al-Nazzam (natures, kumun).
- `positive_sum_cooperation` (Positive-sum cooperation (trade is not zero-sum)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Merchants and partnership law (mudaraba) assume both sides gain from trade; the Prophet himself was a merchant. Courtiers think of revenue as the caliph's share of a fixed harvest.
- `reproducibility_open_publication` (Reproducibility and open publication): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Paper and the Suq al-Warraqin make copying cheaper here than in Byzantium or Latin Europe. Translations are commissioned, revised and circulated; observations are written into zijes others can recompute. Knowledge still flows through patrons and teaching circles. Local: Suq al-Warraqin; Khizanat al-Hikma (Sahl ibn Harun).
- `thought_experiment` (Thought experiment): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Kalam is full of hypothetical cases, and al-Nazzam argues that a body crossing infinitely divisible space must 'leap' (tafra). Mu'tazila and jurists reason freely from imagined cases. Local: Ibrahim al-Nazzam; Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf.
- `tragedy_of_the_commons` (Commons problem and how communities solve it): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Water law is detailed, with rules on shares of canal water, the right to drink and to irrigate, and reserved pastures (hima). Over-irrigation salts the southern Sawad, a commons failure nobody connects to its cause. Local: qadis and canal officials of the Sawad.
- `empiricism_over_authority` (Test claims instead of trusting authority): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Al-Ma'mun's astronomers call their tables 'verified' because they checked Ptolemy, and the Mu'tazila put reason before tradition in theology. In medicine Galen and Hippocrates still decide; al-Razi's Doubts about Galen is c. 900. Local: Yahya ibn Abi Mansur; Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf, al-Nazzam (Mu'tazila).
- `mathematical_laws_of_nature` (Nature follows simple mathematical laws): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The heavens are believed to move by geometry; Ptolemy is being re-translated and checked. On earth, motion, weight and heat are explained by Aristotle's qualities, not by number. Al-Kindi will argue for mathematics as the way into philosophy. Local: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi; al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar (Almagest).
- `scientific_method` (Scientific method (conjecture, test, publish, repeat)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Al-Ma'mun's program of new observations to check Ptolemy and the Indian tables is a state-funded test of received numbers, rare in the world. The idea that an experiment decides between theories of nature is not yet stated; Ibn al-Haytham is two centuries away. Local: Yahya ibn Abi Mansur and the Mumtahan (verified) tables; al-Ma'mun.
- `freedom_of_speech_thought` (Freedom of thought, speech and the press): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Al-Ma'mun hosts debates between theologians and faiths and enjoys argument. In spring 833 he begins the Mihna, testing qadis and scholars on the createdness of the Quran. Open dissent from the caliph's doctrine is about to become dangerous. Local: al-Ma'mun; Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad; Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
- `cognitive_biases` (Systematic errors of human judgement (cognitive biases)): K1 use:none make:easy acc:low. Hadith critics know that partisanship, piety and invention distort reports. A general account of how judgement errs does not exist.
- `correlation_causation_confounding` (Correlation, causation and confounding): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Aristotle's Topics and Analytics distinguish essential from accidental connection, read in Syriac by Christian scholars. Astrologers infer causes from coincidences daily.
- `fallibilism_provisional_knowledge` (Fallibilism (all knowledge of nature is provisional)): K1 use:none make:easy acc:low. Kalam debaters argue both sides and switch positions; Greek sceptical arguments are known by report. Revealed knowledge is held certain, and the createdness of the Quran is about to be enforced as certain too.
- `game_theory` (Game theory (prisoner's dilemma, credible commitment)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Chess (shatranj) is the court game and a metaphor for strategy; Persian mirrors for princes teach the calculation of alliances. No theory of strategic choice.
- `idea_of_progress` (Idea of progress (knowledge accumulates, the future can be better)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Al-Ma'mun's men believe they can improve on Ptolemy's numbers, and al-Kindi will say one should take truth from whoever brought it. History is otherwise read as a decline from the Prophet's generation. Local: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi.
- `informed_consent_research_ethics` (Consent and ethics of experiments on people): K1 use:none make:easy acc:low. The Hippocratic Oath is known to Christian physicians. Al-Ruhawi's Ethics of the Physician comes later in the century. Slaves, prisoners and the poor have no say in what is done to them.
- `occams_razor` (Parsimony (Occam's razor)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Aristotle's maxim that nature does nothing in vain is known; Mu'tazila argue from simplicity of explanation as a debating rule.
- `scepticism_superstition` (Scepticism towards astrology, omens, witchcraft and transmutation): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Astrology is a court profession; al-Ma'mun's astronomers also cast horoscopes and advise on campaigns. Some jurists condemn it as forbidden divination, for religious rather than empirical reasons. Alchemy is a serious craft. Local: Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (now a hadith man hostile to the philosophers); court astrologers.
- `social_contract` (Social contract (government by consent)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The caliph rules by pledge of allegiance (bay'a), sworn and sometimes broken; the civil war of 811–813 was fought over it. The idea that rule is a contract with the ruled is a jurist's theory of later centuries.
- `systematic_invention` (Invention as a method (organised research and development)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The caliph pays a team, instruments and books to produce new astronomical tables, and the palace library employs copyists and translators. Nobody applies this to machines or medicine. Local: al-Ma'mun's observation program (Shammasiyya 828–829, Qasiyun 831–833).
- `utilitarianism` (Utilitarianism (judge rules by their consequences for everyone)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Jurists weigh 'the public good' (maslaha) and 'preference' (istihsan) in the Hanafi school; never as a general rule above revelation. Local: Hanafi jurists at court (Yahya ibn Aktham).
- `abolition_of_torture` (Abolition of judicial torture; proportionate, certain punishment): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Jurists hold that a confession under duress is invalid, yet police and caliphs flog and imprison, and rebels are crucified on the bridges as a display. Ibn Hanbal will be flogged under the Mihna. - `mechanical_philosophy` (Mechanical philosophy (explain by matter and motion, not hidden purposes)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Greek automata texts entertain courtiers; nobody thinks the world itself works like one. For the kalam atomists the world has no causes of its own at all, only God's habit.
- `bayesian_reasoning` (Weighing evidence (base rates and Bayesian updating)): K0 make:easy acc:low
- `controlled_trial` (Controlled comparison (experiment with control group)): K0 make:easy acc:low. Physicians test drugs by tradition and on single patients. - `placebo_blinding` (Placebo effect and blinded trials): K0 make:easy acc:low
- `selection_bias_sampling` (Selection and survivorship bias, fair sampling): K0 make:easy acc:low
- `falsifiability` (Falsifiability (risky, testable predictions)): K0 make:medium acc:low. A failed horoscope is blamed on a wrong birth time. Only the astronomers expose their predictions to a check, by timing eclipses. Local: Habash al-Hasib (eclipse computations).
- `natural_rights` (Natural (human) rights): K0 make:medium acc:low. Rights come from God's law, not nature. Jurists protect life and property for Muslims and, by contract, dhimmis.
- `universal_physical_laws` (The same physical laws on earth and in the heavens): K0 make:hard acc:low. Aristotle's heavens are of a fifth element, unchanging and moving in circles; the sublunar world is different in kind. Nobody here questions it.
- `secular_state` (Secular state (separation of religious and civil authority)): K0 make:very-hard acc:low. The caliph is the commander of the faithful. ## Agriculture & food (`agriculture`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/agriculture.md)
- `food_preservation` (Food preservation (salting, drying, smoking, pickling)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Dates are dried and pressed into blocks or boiled to syrup (dibs); fish is salted and sun-dried; vegetables are pickled in vinegar; murri, a fermented barley sauce, is a staple of cookery; sugar and honey preserve fruit. Local: Basra date packers; cooks and confectioners of the court.
- `grafting_fruit_trees` (Grafting of fruit trees and vines): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Gardeners graft citrus, apricots, pears and vines routinely, following Persian practice and Greek farming books known through Syriac. Local: palace gardens on the east bank (Shammasiyya, Rusafa).
- `irrigation_water_lifting` (Irrigation and water lifting (canal, qanat, shaduf, noria)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The Sawad lives on a Sasanian canal grid (Nahrawan, Nahr Isa, Sarat), with sluices, shadufs, animal-driven saqiyas and river-driven norias. Iran waters its towns by qanats. Upkeep is a state task; neglect and salt are the threats. Local: Nahr Isa and Sarat canals, Baghdad; Nahrawan canal east of the Tigris; officials who assess and repair the canals. Elsewhere: Khurasan and Fars, qanats.
- `sugar_cane_beet` (Sugar from cane and from beet): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Cane is grown and boiled in Khuzistan, a crop since Sasanian times, and refined into loaves and rock candy (qand). Sugar is a luxury, a medicine and the base of court confectionery. Beet sugar is unknown. Local: Khuzistan cane fields (Ahvaz, Gondeshapur); sugar-sellers in the Baghdad markets.
- `wet_rice_cultivation` (Wet rice (paddy) cultivation): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Rice is a staple around Wasit, in the southern marshes (the Batiha) and in Khuzistan; the poor of Basra eat rice bread. It is spreading west to Egypt and beyond. Local: Wasit and the Batiha marshes; Khuzistan.
- `grain_storage_pest_control` (Grain storage and protection from pests and ergot): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Grain is kept in pits, jars and state granaries; tax grain feeds the army and the capital. Weevils and rats are accepted losses. Ergot is no issue; rye is not grown.
- `manure_compost_night_soil` (Manure, compost and night soil): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. - `sounding_lead_pilotage` (Sounding lead, rutters and coastal pilotage): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The Shatt al-Arab and the Gulf are full of shoals; pilots sound with lead and line and pass on landmarks orally. Written rutters come centuries later. Local: pilots at Ubulla and Abbadan.
- `stirrup_saddle` (Saddle, stirrups and horseshoes): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Iron stirrups have been standard since the late 7th century; saddles are built on wooden trees. Whether horses are shod with nailed shoes is uncertain.
- `latitude_astrolabe_quadrant` (Latitude from Pole Star and noon Sun (quadrant, astrolabe, cross-staff, kamal)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Court astronomers take latitude with astrolabes and quadrants, and the Mumtahan tables give town latitudes. Pilots judge the Pole Star's height by eye; a finger-scaled sighting board is attested only later. Local: Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi; Sanad ibn Ali.
- `lighthouse_buoys` (Lighthouses and buoys): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The Pharos of Alexandria still stands. Later writers describe wooden beacon platforms (khashabat) in the sea off Abbadan, lit at night for ships entering the Tigris; whether they stand yet is unknown. Elsewhere: Alexandria, the Pharos.
- `ship_provisioning_long_voyages` (Provisioning and keeping crews alive on long voyages): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Ships to China stop at Muscat, Quilon and the Malay ports for water and food; dates, rice and dried fish keep. Scurvy is rare on these hops.
- `tides_tide_tables` (Tides and tide tables): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Basra's canals fill and empty twice a day with the tide of the Shatt al-Arab, and boatmen and millers time their work by it. The tie to the moon is noticed; a theory and tables are not. Local: Basra's tidal canals.
- `wind_systems_ocean_currents` (Global wind belts and ocean currents (trade winds, westerlies, volta do mar, monsoon)): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Gulf captains time their voyages to India and China by the monsoon and count a round trip to China in a year or more. The global wind belts and the Atlantic are beyond anyone's horizon. Local: ship captains (nakhuda) and pilots of Basra, Ubulla and Siraf.
- `arch_bridge_truss` (Bridges (arch, truss, suspension)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:high. Baghdad crosses the Tigris on pontoon bridges of boats chained together. Sasanian masonry bridges and bridge-dams survive in Khuzistan (Shushtar). Truss and suspension bridges are unknown. Local: pontoon bridges between Karkh, Rusafa and Shammasiyya. Elsewhere: Shushtar, Sasanian bridge-dam.
- `world_geography` (The real layout of the world (continents, oceans, sea routes)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:high. The earth is a sphere; al-Ma'mun's astronomers measure a degree. Al-Khwarizmi is recasting Ptolemy's coordinates in his Picture of the Earth, and a world map is drawn for the caliph. Merchants know the sea route to China; the Encircling Sea bounds the west. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; al-Ma'mun's world map (al-sura al-ma'muniyya); Basra and Siraf merchants who have been to Khanfu (Guangzhou). Elsewhere: Tang China.
- `copper_sheathing_shipworm` (Shipworm and copper sheathing): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Shipworm and rot are a constant cost in warm seas; hulls are smeared with oil and lime (described by later writers). Copper is expensive and would need nails a sewn hull does not have.
- `dead_reckoning_log_line` (Dead reckoning (course, speed, time; log line and traverse table)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Pilots keep courses by star bearings and reckon distance in days' sail, from memory and oral rutters. No log line, no sandglass, no compass.
- `map_projection_charts` (Nautical charts and map projections (portolans, Ptolemy, Mercator)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Ptolemy's Geography, with grids and projections, is available in translation and reworked by al-Khwarizmi. Sailors carry no charts; route lists and memory serve. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.
- `paved_roads_macadam` (Engineered roads (Roman roads to macadam)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The Khurasan road and the pilgrim road to Mecca (Darb Zubayda, with cisterns and stations) are tracks with wells and inns, not paved. Camel caravans need no pavement. Local: Khurasan road from Baghdad's eastern gate; Darb Zubayda to Mecca.
- `spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage` (Spoked wheels, pivoting axles and sprung carriages): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Spoked wheels are known, but carts are rare; the camel carries more cheaply on these roads. Women of rank travel in litters on camels or mules.
- `longitude_lunar_distances` (Longitude by lunar distances): K2 use:none make:very-hard acc:low. Ptolemy's method of timing one lunar eclipse in two places is known, and the caliph's astronomers care about longitudes. Lunar tables and instruments are far too coarse for use at sea. Local: Habash al-Hasib.
- `canal_locks` (Canals and pound locks): K1 use:none make:medium acc:medium. Iraq's canals are flat and fed by sluices and weirs; boats are towed. A pound lock is unknown and would mainly help where canals cross a level change.
- `diving_bell` (Diving bell and underwater work): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Pearl divers of the Gulf dive on held breath with nose clips and a weighted line. Alexander's descent in a glass vessel is a story in the Alexander romance. Elsewhere: Bahrain and the Gulf pearl banks.
- `chinese_junk_treasure_ships` (Chinese junk and Zheng He's treasure fleets): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Merchants back from Khanfu talk of large Chinese ships and iron-nailed hulls. Zheng He's fleets are six centuries away. Elsewhere: Tang China, Guangzhou.

## Communication & information (`communication`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/communication.md)
- `alphabet_writing` (Alphabet and mass literacy): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Arabic script now carries dots and vowel signs; Syriac, Hebrew and Pahlavi are written alongside. Many town men can read a little; secretaries, scholars and merchants read well. Mass literacy is no one's aim.
- `codex_book` (Codex book and finding aids): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Books are paper or parchment codices copied by professional stationers (warraqin) in the booksellers' market. Paper makes books cheaper every decade. Local: Suq al-Warraqin (booksellers' market), Baghdad; Baghdad paper makers.
- `postal_system` (Relay post and public mail): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The barid runs relay stations with mules and riders along the main roads; its masters in each province report on governors to the caliph. It is a state service, not public mail; private letters go with travellers and merchants. Local: the diwan al-barid.
- `vernacular_translation` (Knowledge in the vernacular; translation movements): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. This is the translation movement at its height. Greek works come into Arabic, often through Syriac, alongside Pahlavi and Sanskrit, paid for by the caliph, officials, physicians and private patrons. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar; Hunayn ibn Ishaq (young, learning Greek); Yuhanna ibn Masawayh; the Khizanat al-Hikma (Bayt al-Hikma).
- `writing_invention` (Writing (signs that record language)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high
- `encyclopedia_reference_works` (Encyclopedias and dictionaries): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Al-Khalil's Kitab al-Ayn, the first Arabic dictionary (late 8th c.), orders words by sound; Sibawayh's grammar is the standard. Encyclopedias of the sciences come later.
- `pencil_steel_pen` (Pencil, steel pen and durable ink): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Writing is done with cut reed pens (qalam), soot ink (midad) and iron-gall ink. Calligraphers argue about how to cut the nib; a pen with its own reservoir is a 10th-century novelty in Egypt.
- `library_catalogue` (Library catalogue and classification): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. The caliph's Khizanat al-Hikma has librarians and copyists; stationers keep lists of what they can copy. No union catalogue; Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist is 150 years away. Local: Sahl ibn Harun, keeper of the Khizanat al-Hikma.
- `sign_languages` (Sign languages of deaf people): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Jurists accept the intelligible gestures of a mute person for contracts, divorce and oaths; deaf people sign at home. There is no taught sign language.
- `signal_beacons_flag_codes` (Beacons, flag codes and heliograph): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Fire and smoke signals are used on the frontiers and coasts. Across the border, the Byzantines run a beacon chain from the Cilician frontier to Constantinople. Elsewhere: Byzantine beacon chain (later linked to Leo the Mathematician).
- `shorthand` (Shorthand (stenography)): K1 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Secretaries abbreviate in the diwans, and Byzantine notaries know Greek tachygraphy. Dictation is slowed by the reed pen.
- `scientific_journal` (Scientific journal and peer review): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Scholars answer each other in epistles (rasa'il) and dispute in the caliph's assemblies (majalis). Nothing periodic, and nobody reviews before copying. Local: al-Ma'mun's debating sessions.
- `braille_tactile_writing` (Braille (tactile writing for blind people)): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Blind men are respected Quran reciters and scholars who learn by ear and memory.
- `standard_time_zones` (Standard time and time zones): K0 make:easy acc:low. Time is local and set by the sun; the hours of prayer follow shadow length and sunset. Astronomers know noon differs with longitude.
- `woodblock_printing` (Woodblock printing): K0 make:easy acc:low. Paper, soot ink and carved seals all exist; block-printed charms appear in Egypt only in the 10th century. Printing the Quran would offend those who see copying it as devotion. Elsewhere: Tang China, printed charms, sutras and calendars.
- `copying_duplicating` (Copying documents (copying press, carbon paper, stencil duplicator)): K0 make:medium acc:medium. Every copy is written by hand; a large book takes a copyist weeks.
- `lithography_engraving` (Reproducing images (woodcut, engraving, etching, lithography)): K0 make:medium acc:low. Seal cutters engrave stones and dies for coins; nobody prints images.
- `newspapers_periodicals` (Newspapers and periodicals): K0 make:medium acc:low. News travels by the caliph's letters, read out in the mosques at Friday prayer, and by the barid.
- `optical_telegraph` (Optical telegraph (semaphore network)): K0 make:medium acc:low
- `printing_press` (Movable-type printing press): K0 make:hard acc:low. Joined Arabic letters change shape by position, so movable type needs hundreds of sorts. No screw press for paper, no type metal.

## Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/institutions.md)
- `commercial_law_contract_enforcement` (Contracts, notaries and merchant courts): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The Quran orders debts to be written and witnessed; qadis enforce sale, hire, partnership and agency, and formularies for deeds are circulating. Jurists already sell legal devices (hiyal) around the ban on interest. Local: Karkh markets; Hanafi jurists at the qadi's court.
- `standard_weights_measures` (Standard weights and measures): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Coin weights are legal standards (mithqal, dirham); market inspectors test scales, and stamped glass weights are made in Egypt. The ratl and the grain measures differ between Baghdad, Kufa and Basra. Local: the market inspector (sahib al-suq, muhtasib); money changers of Karkh.
- `charitable_endowment_waqf` (Perpetual endowment (waqf, foundation, trust)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Pious foundations fund wells, mosques and the poor. Jurists still dispute whether an endowment is irrevocable (Abu Yusuf yes, Abu Hanifa no); the doctrine is being written now. Local: Zubayda's waterworks on the Mecca road.
- `census_vital_registration` (Census and registration of births and deaths): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The army register lists each soldier by name, father and physical description, and tax registers list the dhimmis who owe jizya. Nobody records births, deaths or causes. Local: diwan al-jund (army bureau).
- `fire_brigade_police_building_codes` (Fire brigade, civil police and building rules): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The shurta polices Baghdad and the gates are shut at night; quarters have watchmen. Markets of reed and wood burn; the inspector polices encroachment on streets. The 'ayyarun gangs of the civil war still rule some alleys. Local: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi; Karkh markets.
- `international_law_sovereignty` (Treaties, diplomacy and international law): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Al-Shaybani's Siyar (d. 805) sets out war, truce and safe-conduct (aman). Envoys pass to Constantinople and prisoners are exchanged on the Lamos river in Cilicia (805; the next exchange only in 845). Byzantium is an enemy to be bled, not an equal. Elsewhere: Constantinople, Emperor Theophilos (r. 829–842).
- `property_rights_land_registry` (Secure property rights and land registry): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The Sawad has been surveyed for land tax since the conquest and the tax bureau keeps registers. Title rests on witnesses and deeds; fallen officials and their families have everything confiscated (the Barmakids in 803). Local: diwan al-kharaj (land-tax bureau); professional witnesses ('udul) at the qadi's court.
- `public_accounts_audit` (Public accounts, audit and budget): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. A control bureau (diwan al-zimam) checks the other bureaus' accounts; revenue lists by province exist. The usual audit is to arrest a dismissed secretary and squeeze him for what he took. Local: diwan al-zimam; the caliph's secretaries (kuttab).
- `social_insurance` (Social insurance and poor relief): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Zakat and alms go to the poor, debtors and travellers; registered soldiers draw stipends; the bimaristan treats without fee. Relief is charity or pay, not a fund with contributions.
- `universal_schooling` (Universal elementary schooling): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Quran schools (kuttab) teach boys to read and write for a fee, and literacy is unusually common among townsmen. Girls are taught at home if at all; nothing is free or compulsory.
- `written_law_code` (Written, published law code): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Law is the jurists' reading of Quran and Prophetic precedent, not a code the ruler enacts. Ibn al-Muqaffa' urged al-Mansur (c. 750s) to impose one uniform code; jurists still resist. Al-Shafi'i (d. 820) has just systematised the sources. Local: Yahya ibn Aktham, chief qadi; Ahmad ibn Hanbal; pupils of Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani (Hanafi school). Elsewhere: Constantinople, the Ecloga (741) and Justinian's Code; Tang China, the Tang Code (653).
- `guilds_apprenticeship` (Craft guilds and apprenticeship): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Each craft has its own street or market with a headman ('arif) answerable to the inspector. Crafts pass from father to son; whether self-governing guilds exist is disputed by historians.
- `habeas_corpus_fair_trial` (Habeas corpus and fair trial): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Before a qadi the claimant must prove with two upright witnesses and fixed penalties are averted by doubt. The police and the caliph imprison without any qadi, and torture for confession or taxes is routine. Local: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi, chief of police; the Matbaq, the caliphs' state prison.
- `merit_civil_service` (Merit-based civil service (examinations)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Secretaries are trained in Arabic style, accounts and Persian manners, often in secretary families (many of them Persian or Christian); entry is by patronage. No examinations. Elsewhere: Tang China, the civil-service examinations.
- `public_library_museum` (Public library and museum): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The caliph's library is open by favour to scholars and copyists; great men keep private libraries. The real public access is the booksellers' market, where books can be read or copied for a fee. Local: Khizanat al-Hikma; Suq al-Warraqin. Elsewhere: Constantinople, the patriarchal and imperial libraries.
- `scientific_academy` (Scientific society or academy): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The Bayt al-Hikma is the caliph's library and bureau, not an academy. Al-Ma'mun's court comes close, with funded observers, instruments, recorded results (the 'verified' tables) and debates in his majlis. It all depends on one patron. Local: Khizanat al-Hikma (Sahl ibn Harun, Salm); Yahya ibn Abi Mansur, Sanad ibn Ali, Habash al-Hasib; the caliph's majlis.
- `independent_judiciary_judicial_review` (Independent judges and judicial review): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Qadis judge by a law the caliph did not make, but he appoints and dismisses them, and the Mihna will examine every qadi on the createdness of the Quran. Grievances against officials go to the ruler's own mazalim hearings. Local: Yahya ibn Aktham; the caliph's mazalim (grievance) sessions.
- `peaceful_transfer_of_power` (Peaceful transfer of power and loyal opposition): K2 use:wrong make:hard acc:low. Harun's succession pact of 802, written and hung in the Kaaba, ended in civil war and al-Amin's death in 813. Al-Ma'mun named the Alid Ali al-Rida heir in 817 (dead 818). In 833 he passes over his son for his brother. Local: Abu Ishaq al-Mu'tasim; al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun; Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi (anti-caliph 817–819, pardoned).
- `rule_of_law` (Rule of law and separation of powers): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Everyone agrees God's law stands above the caliph; nobody agrees who interprets it. Al-Ma'mun claims that authority for himself, and the Mihna of 833 is the test. Officials answer to him, not to courts. Local: Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad (the caliph's party); Ahmad ibn Hanbal (the scholars' party).
- `women_rights_suffrage` (Women's legal rights and suffrage): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. A free woman owns and keeps her property and dower, contracts and can sue; she inherits half a brother's share and is secluded if well-born. Zubayda, Harun's widow, funds wells and cisterns along the pilgrim road until her death (831). Local: Zubayda bint Ja'far; Buran, al-Ma'mun's wife (wedding at Fam al-Silh, 825/826); trained singing slave girls (qiyan).
- `sortition` (Selection of officials by lot (sortition)): K1 use:partial make:easy acc:low. Drawing lots (qur'a) is lawful for dividing shares or settling equal claims, after Prophetic precedent. Filling an office by lot would look like gambling with God's trust.
- `public_health_board` (Permanent public health authority): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The market inspector checks bread, meat and weights, and the bimaristan cares for some of the sick. No one counts deaths or orders isolation; epidemics are God's decree. Local: the market inspector; the bimaristan of Harun's reign.
- `citizen_assembly` (Direct democracy (citizen assembly voting on laws)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. The Friday mosque is where policy is announced, not decided. Crowds act in riots and in the Baghdad vigilante movement of 817; Athens is a name in Greek books.
- `federalism_subsidiarity` (Federalism and subsidiarity): K1 use:partial make:hard acc:low. In practice the Tahirids hold Khurasan by inheritance and the Aghlabids rule Ifriqiya for a tribute. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians run family law and worship under their own heads. Local: Abdallah ibn Tahir, governor of Khurasan; the Catholicos of the Church of the East; the Jewish Exilarch in Baghdad.
- `industrial_research_lab` (Organised industrial research laboratory): K1 use:partial make:hard acc:low. The observation programmes at Shammasiyya (828–829) and Mt Qasiyun (831–833) are a staffed, funded long programme, ending when al-Ma'mun dies. Nothing similar exists for crafts. Local: Shammasiyya observatory, Baghdad; Mt Qasiyun, Damascus (Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Marwarrudhi).
- `representative_government` (Representative government (elected assembly)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Consultation (shura) is praised and means the ruler hearing his chosen counsellors. Allegiance (bay'a) is sworn by notables to a man already designated. No body is elected, and Aristotle's Politics is not translated.
- `university` (University (self-governing body of teachers and students)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Teaching happens in study circles in mosques and houses, around one master, with licences to transmit. No chartered body of teachers, no degree; the endowed madrasa is two centuries away.
- `written_constitution` (Written constitution): K1 use:partial make:hard acc:low. The Medina pact is preserved in the Prophet's biography; Harun's Mecca documents were a written settlement of power, and they failed. A charter that binds the caliph himself is unthought. Local: Ibn Sa'd and the biographers of the Prophet in Baghdad.
- `abolition_of_slavery` (Abolition of slavery): K1 use:none make:very-hard acc:low. Freeing slaves is a pious act, slaves may buy their freedom by contract, and a concubine who bears her master a child goes free at his death. Al-Ma'mun's own mother was a slave. Abolition is unthinkable. Local: slave market (dar al-raqiq) in Baghdad; Zanj labourers in the Basra salt flats.
- `copyright` (Copyright for authors): K0 make:easy acc:low. Any copyist in the stationers' market may copy any book. The scholarly answer is transmission by audition and licence (ijaza), which protects accuracy, not income. Local: Suq al-Warraqin (stationers' market).
- `secret_ballot` (Secret ballot): K0 make:easy acc:low. Nothing is voted on. Paper and sealed boxes would make it trivial to run, if any body existed that chose by votes.
- `patents` (Patent law): K0 make:medium acc:low. An inventor's reward is a caliph's gift or a post. Craftsmen guard secrets in the family, and a monopoly would need a caliphal grant.

- `free_press` (Freedom of the press): K0 make:hard acc:low. No press. Books circulate freely unless they touch religion; al-Mahdi hunted 'zindiqs' in the 780s, and from 833 the Mihna makes a doctrine compulsory for officials and scholars.

## Economy & finance (`economy`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/economy.md)
- `coinage` (Coinage (stamped metal money)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Gold dinar (about 4.25 g), silver dirham (about 2.9 g), copper fulus for small change, all purely inscribed. Al-Ma'mun's reform type of the 820s adds a Quran verse in the outer margin. Big sums are weighed; money changers profit on the rate. Local: mint of Madinat al-Salam; money changers (sarrafun) of Karkh.
- `partnership_commenda` (Risk-sharing partnership (commenda, mudaraba)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Mudaraba (qirad) is standard, worked out by the Hanafis (al-Shaybani); the investor bears the loss, the agent his labour. Partnerships carry Basra's trade to India and China. Local: Basra and Siraf merchants.
- `division_of_labour` (Division of labour and specialisation): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Baghdad's markets are divided street by street by trade, from paper to perfume. Plato's point that a city needs many specialists is known. No one has taken a single trade apart into steps. Local: Karkh markets; paper makers and copyists.
- `interest_loans_collateral` (Interest-bearing loans, pledges and limits on debt bondage): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Interest (riba) is forbidden, so credit runs through deferred-price sales, advance purchase (salam), pledges and double-sale tricks. A qadi may jail a debtor who can pay and will not.
- `price_mechanism_supply_demand` (Prices, supply and demand): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. A hadith has the Prophet refuse to fix prices ('God is the one who sets them'); hoarding food is condemned. Governors still fix grain prices in a crisis.
- `banking_credit` (Deposit banking and bills of exchange): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Written payment orders (sakk) are old; the suftaja, a loan repaid in another city, is spreading among merchants and officials. Court bankers (jahbadh) handling state funds are better attested a few decades later. Local: money changers of Karkh; Basra merchants. Elsewhere: Tang China, 'flying money' remittance certificates.
- `ever_normal_granary` (Public granaries and price stabilisation (ever-normal granary)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Everyone knows Joseph storing grain for seven lean years (Quran, sura 12). The state keeps stores for the army and court, not a buffer for prices. Elsewhere: Tang China, ever-normal granaries.
- `progressive_income_tax` (Income tax and progressive rates): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Jizya is graded in three classes by wealth (48, 24 or 12 dirhams a year); zakat takes a fixed share above a threshold; land tax is by area or a share of the crop. Income as such is never assessed. Local: diwan al-kharaj.
- `comparative_advantage_free_trade` (Comparative advantage and free trade): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Egyptian linen, Khurasani cotton, Indian pepper and Chinese silk and stoneware meet in Baghdad. Customs dues are levied at frontiers and ports. Nobody theorises why both sides gain.
- `double_entry` (Double-entry bookkeeping): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Bureaus keep day books and monthly and annual summaries in words, with their own clerks' notation. Two-sided accounts that must balance are not used; merchants keep simple lists of debts. Local: diwan al-zimam.
- `economic_growth_productivity` (Wealth as productivity; sustained economic growth): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The Persian idea that a just ruler's revenue depends on cultivated, prospering land ('imara) is common; Tahir ibn al-Husayn's letter to his son (821) says so. Wealth means land, tax and treasure. Local: Tahir's letter to Abdallah ibn Tahir.
- `insurance` (Insurance (marine, fire, life)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. The aqila kin group shares blood money; seafarers share jettisoned cargo by custom. A paid premium against a chance loss looks to jurists like gambling (gharar, maysir).
- `quantity_theory_inflation` (Money supply, debasement and inflation): K1 use:none make:medium acc:low. Abbasid silver is good, so debasement is not the issue. Prices are blamed on hoarders, bad harvests and war, like the famine of the siege of 812–813. Nobody connects prices with the coin the caliph spends.
- `national_accounts_gdp` (National income accounts (GDP)): K1 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Revenue lists by province, in coin and kind, are a rough map of what the empire produces. Output itself is never counted.
- `public_debt_bonds` (Public debt and government bonds): K1 use:partial make:hard acc:low. The caliph borrows from rich officials and merchants when pay runs out, and tax farmers advance revenue. Nothing is standard, transferable or interest-bearing.
- `cooperatives_savings_banks` (Savings banks, credit and consumer cooperatives): K0 make:medium acc:low. The poor save in jewellery and keep coin with a trusted neighbour or merchant. Interest on deposits would be riba.
- `paper_money` (Paper money): K0 make:medium acc:low. Paper, seals and trusted bureaus exist, so notes could be made. Accepting a slip of paper for silver would need the state to take it back in taxes, and jurists would fear gharar. Elsewhere: Tang China, flying money (not yet currency).
- `aggregate_demand_countercyclical_policy` (Fighting slumps by sustaining demand (Keynesian policy)): K0 make:hard acc:low. Caliphs build canals and palaces for glory and hand out gifts in bad years, not on any theory.
- `joint_stock_company` (Joint-stock company and limited liability): K0 make:hard acc:low. The law knows partners, not a legal person that outlives them. A partnership dissolves at a death, and shares cannot be sold to strangers.
- `life_tables_annuities` (Life tables and the pricing of annuities): K0 make:hard acc:low. Inheritance arithmetic fills half of al-Khwarizmi's al-Jabr, but no one records ages at death, and annuities would run into the ban on interest. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.

- `central_bank` (Central bank and lender of last resort): K0 make:very-hard acc:low. There is the public treasury (bayt al-mal) and the caliph's privy purse, and he spends from both.

## Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/military.md)
- `cavalry_chariot` (Horse warfare (chariot, cavalry, horse archers)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Cavalry is the army, mailed lancers and horse archers on stirrups, and Turkish archers are prized. The chariot is ancient history. Local: al-Afshin, general; Abu Ishaq al-Mu'tasim and his Turkish guards.
- `siegecraft_mining` (Siegecraft, mining and counter-mining): K4 use:correct make:medium acc:high. Mining, rams under sheds, towers and trebuchets are routine on the Byzantine frontier; the Byzantine forts of Cappadocia fall to blockade and assault in 830–832. Local: frontier bases at Tarsus and al-Massisa.
- `torsion_artillery_trebuchet` (Mechanical artillery (torsion catapult, trebuchet)): K4 use:correct make:medium acc:high. Traction trebuchets (manjaniq) pulled by crews, and light 'arrada, shelled Baghdad's houses in 812–813. The counterweight trebuchet is unknown; torsion engines survive in Greek books.
- `deterrence` (Deterrence): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Annual summer raids, punitive campaigns (Harun's against Heraclea in 806) and the threat of a caliph in person keep the frontier in line. Tribute is the price of peace.
- `field_fortification` (Field fortification (marching camp, wagon fort, entrenchment)): K3 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The trench (khandaq) is part of sacred history (Medina, 627); armies ditch their camps and Baghdad's defenders dug in during the siege. Against Babak's mountain strongholds it will need patience.
- `close_order_infantry` (Disciplined close-order infantry (phalanx, legion)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Infantry fight in ranks behind shields and spears to anchor the horsemen; the Baghdad Abna', the old infantry, were broken in 813. Byzantine manuals of drill are unknown here. Elsewhere: Byzantium, Maurice's Strategikon.
- `crossbow_longbow` (Bows of war (composite bow, crossbow, longbow)): K3 use:correct make:medium acc:high. The composite bow of horn, wood and sinew is the main missile weapon, made by specialist bowyers. Hand crossbows are rare here. Elsewhere: Tang China, mass-produced crossbows.
- `incendiaries_greek_fire` (Incendiary weapons and Greek fire): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:high. Naphtha from Iraqi seeps is thrown in pots or on arrows by specialist naphtha men (naffatun). The Byzantine siphon that sprays burning oil from ships is a guarded secret. Elsewhere: Constantinople, Greek fire siphons.
- `laws_of_war` (Laws of war (humanitarian law)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Jurists forbid killing women, children, monks and the old, and grant safe-conduct; al-Shaybani wrote the rules down. Captives are still enslaved or held for ransom and exchange.
- `mercenaries_citizen_militia` (Mercenaries, militias and the loyalty of armed men): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The question is who the army is loyal to. The Khurasanis brought al-Ma'mun to power; Baghdad's Abna' fought him; in 817 citizens formed vigilante militias. Al-Mu'tasim's Turkish slave soldiers are the answer that will arrive. Local: Abu Ishaq al-Mu'tasim; al-Afshin.
- `military_engineering_roads_bridges` (Military engineering (roads, bridges, pioneers)): K3 use:correct make:medium acc:high. Boat bridges span the Tigris at Baghdad; the old Roman and Sasanian roads carry the post. In 833 al-Ma'mun orders Tyana rebuilt as a fortified base.
- `military_intelligence_codebreaking` (Military intelligence and codebreaking): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The postmasters of the barid report on governors and frontiers, and spies cross into Byzantium. Al-Khalil (d. 786) wrote a lost book on secret writing; al-Kindi's frequency analysis is still ahead.
